Idealists control the symbols by the Old Testament background John constantly alludes to (Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah) and by the book's own interpretations, which they argue offers more objective controls than matching symbols to particular current or ancient events.
The structure of Revelation suggests progression (seven seals, then seven trumpets, then seven bowls), not mere repetition, and Revelation 20 follows Revelation 19 sequentially.

Recapitulation advocates note that each series ends with the end of history, that the cosmic catastrophe language reappears at each conclusion, and that Revelation 20:7-10 replays the same final battle as Revelation 19:17-21 and Revelation 16:14-16, using the same Ezekiel 38–39 imagery.
Progressive parallelism
Hendriksen's seven parallel sections (chapters 1–3, 4–7, 8–11, 12–14, 15–16, 17–19, 20–22), each spanning the interadvent age with increasing focus on the end.
Pure (symbolic-spiritual) idealism
Revelation portrays timeless principles with no specific historical referents other than the general conflict of good and evil (Milligan in his strongest statements).
Tyconian-Augustinian spiritual reading
The patristic form: the visions describe the church's present spiritual experience, and the millennium is the reign of Christ and the saints in the church age.
Eclectic (Modified Idealism)
Eclectic
Draw on the strengths of each approach: first-century setting, timeless principles and future consummation.

G. K. Beale calls his approach 'eclectic' or a 'redemptive-historical form of modified idealism': Revelation symbolically portrays the conflict between God and evil across the age between Christ's comings, rooted in the first-century situation and culminating in a real, future return and judgment. Others in this camp describe their method as combining preterist, idealist and futurist insights.

The eclectic approach holds that no single school captures Revelation, and combines their valid insights. With preterism it reads the book against its first-century background (Roman imperial power, the emperor cult, pressures on the seven churches); with idealism it sees the symbols as transcending any one fulfilment and recurring throughout the church age; with futurism it affirms that the book climaxes in the yet-future return of Christ, final judgment and new creation; and some allow historicist-style fulfilments in particular events. G. K. Beale's major NIGTC commentary (1999) is the leading example, holding that apart from the final coming of Christ the book does not predict specific historical events beyond some fulfilments for particular churches. Steve Gregg's Revelation: Four Views lays out the four classical approaches side by side, and many contemporary commentators, including Richard Bauckham and Craig Keener, combine first-century reference with transhistorical application and future hope.
Revelation must first be read as a letter to seven real first-century churches (Revelation 1:4, 11), against the background of Roman power and the imperial cult.
Its symbols, drawn from Old Testament prophecy (Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Exodus plagues), typically depict recurring realities rather than one-off events, so they apply throughout the church age.
The 'last days' began with Christ's death and resurrection (inaugurated eschatology), so the book describes the whole interadvent period as eschatological.
The visions largely recapitulate, presenting the same age from different angles, while moving toward a climax.
The book culminates in the real, future, personal return of Christ, the final judgment and the new heavens and earth (Revelation 19:11–22:5).
Method should be governed by careful exegesis of each passage rather than by a single system imposed on the whole book.

Commentators have long mixed approaches. Many older works combine an Olivet preterism with an idealist or futurist Revelation, and George Ladd described his own commentary (1972) as a blend of preterist and futurist methods.

G. K. Beale's The Book of Revelation (NIGTC) argued at length for an eclectic, 'redemptive-historical form of modified idealism', heavily attentive to Old Testament allusions; a condensed Revelation: A Shorter Commentary followed in 2015 with David Campbell.

Steve Gregg's Revelation: Four Views (1997, revised 2013) set preterist, historicist, futurist and spiritual (idealist) readings in parallel columns verse by verse, encouraging readers to weigh each, and C. Marvin Pate's Four Views on the Book of Revelation (1998) staged a similar conversation.

Richard Bauckham's The Theology of the Book of Revelation (1993) and The Climax of Prophecy read the book as prophetic critique of Rome with universal theological significance and future hope, and Craig Keener's NIV Application Commentary combines historical background with ongoing application and a future consummation. Many recent evangelical commentators describe their approach in similar mixed terms.
Honours the genuine insights of each school rather than forcing a single grid onto a complex book.
Grounds the symbols in the first-century setting while preserving relevance for every generation.
Keeps the creedal future hope of Christ's return, resurrection and judgment clearly in view.
Driven by detailed attention to Old Testament background, which is the main source of Revelation's imagery.
Reflects the current direction of much evangelical and broader scholarship on Revelation.
Eclecticism can be arbitrary: the interpreter chooses which approach to apply to each passage, so results may reflect preference rather than method.

Advocates answer that exegesis of each passage, controlled by genre, Old Testament allusion and the book's own structure, determines the reading, and that any single-system approach is more likely to impose an external grid.
Beale's modified idealism is criticised for arguing mainly by critique of other systems and for underplaying the specific near-time indicators ('soon', 'near') that preterists stress.

Beale reads 'soon' and 'near' in the light of inaugurated eschatology: the end-time events began at the cross and resurrection and are already in progress, so the language is fulfilled without requiring a single first-century event.
Futurists object that blending approaches dilutes the book's specific predictions about a future tribulation and Antichrist; preterists object that it dilutes the specific prophecy of AD 70.

Eclectic interpreters reply that recurring patterns can include both intense first-century expressions and a climactic final expression (as 1 John 2:18 speaks of many antichrists and a coming Antichrist), so the approach accommodates both concerns.
Redemptive-historical modified idealism
Beale: the visions symbolise the conflict across the interadvent age with no specific predicted events except the final coming and a few church-specific fulfilments.
Preterist-futurist blend
The book addresses first-century crises (Rome, persecution) that foreshadow a climactic future fulfilment (Ladd's self-description; many evangelical commentators).
Preterist-idealist blend
Revelation critiques first-century Rome and its imperial cult, and its symbols apply to every later empire that claims divine honours, with a future consummation (broadly Bauckham-style readings).
Postmillennialism
Postmil
Christ returns after a long age in which the gospel wins the nations.

Postmillennialists call their view an “eschatology of victory” or an “eschatology of hope.” They speak of the Great Commission as a promise as well as a command: the risen Christ already reigns, and through the Spirit-empowered preaching of the gospel he will disciple the nations, so that the knowledge of the Lord fills the earth before he returns. Many describe it as “optimistic amillennialism”: the same present reign of Christ, expected to bear visible fruit in history.

Postmillennialism holds that Christ's kingdom was inaugurated at his first coming and will grow, by ordinary means of grace rather than by a new dispensation, until the great majority of humanity and the nations are converted and a long era of righteousness and peace prevails. Christ returns after (post-) this millennial era for one general resurrection and judgment. Some postmillennialists identify the millennium with the whole inter-advent age; others with a future “latter-day glory” within it. Many, following the Puritans and Jonathan Edwards, expect a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Israel (Romans 11:12, 15, 25-26) as a trigger of still greater blessing among the Gentiles.

Christ was enthroned at his resurrection and ascension (Psalm 110:1; Matthew 28:18) and now reigns over all things, putting his enemies under his feet until the last enemy, death, is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:24-26).
The millennium of Revelation 20 is a long (symbolic) period within the present age, before the Second Coming; Satan is bound so that he can no longer deceive the nations or halt the gospel's advance.
The kingdom grows gradually and pervasively, like the mustard seed and the leaven (Matthew 13:31-33), and the stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth (Daniel 2:35, 44-45).

The Great Commission will succeed: the nations, not merely individuals out of them, will be discipled, so that “the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord” (Isaiah 11:9; Habakkuk 2:14; Psalm 22:27).
This victory comes through the Spirit, the preached Word, prayer, the sacraments and faithful suffering, not by political coercion or a visible reign of Christ on earth.
Many postmillennialists expect a future mass conversion of ethnic Israel (Romans 11:12, 15, 25-26), which Paul calls “life from the dead” for the world.
Evil is not eradicated: a brief final apostasy or rebellion (Revelation 20:7-10) may precede the end, and history is never sinless before the consummation.
Christ returns once, after the millennium, to raise the righteous and the wicked together, conduct the final judgment and usher in the new heavens and new earth (John 5:28-29; 2 Peter 3:10-13).

Postmillennialists find seeds of their hope in patristic confidence that the gospel would subdue the nations (e.g. Origen's expectation that the gospel would prevail, and Eusebius's after Constantine) and especially in Augustine's identification of the millennium with the church age, which supplied the structure later postmillennialists extended with a more optimistic expectation.

Calvin's commentaries display strong hope for the kingdom's spread (whether he was postmillennial is debated). Martin Bucer and Theodore Beza taught a future conversion of the Jews from Romans 11, a theme that became a seedbed for later postmillennial hope.

English and Scottish Puritans (Thomas Brightman, John Owen, Samuel Rutherford and others) expected a latter-day glory with the calling of the Jews and the fullness of the Gentiles. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 191) prays for both, and the Savoy Declaration (1658) speaks of a more peaceful and glorious condition of the church in the latter days. Daniel Whitby (1703) gave the view a systematic form; Iain Murray's The Puritan Hope traces this tradition.

Jonathan Edwards' A History of the Work of Redemption and his revival writings framed the Great Awakening as a foretaste of millennial glory. The modern missionary movement, including William Carey's Enquiry (1792), drew heavily on this expectation that missions would succeed.

Postmillennialism was the dominant view in American and British Protestantism: Princeton theologians Charles Hodge, A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield, Southern Presbyterians such as Robert Dabney and James Henley Thornwell, and David Brown's Christ's Second Coming (1846). Later, liberal 'social gospel' versions secularised the hope, which conservative postmillennialists regard as a distortion.

After the world wars the view declined, but it revived through Loraine Boettner's The Millennium (1957), Iain Murray (1971), R. J. Rushdoony and Greg Bahnsen (Christian Reconstruction), and later Kenneth Gentry's He Shall Have Dominion, Keith Mathison's Postmillennialism: An Eschatology of Hope, Gary DeMar and Douglas Wilson. Proponents report renewed interest among Reformed Presbyterians and Baptists today.

Takes seriously the many Old Testament promises that all nations will worship the Lord and the Messiah's rule will extend to the ends of the earth, reading them as fulfilled within history and not only after it.
Coheres with the New Testament's simple 'one return, one resurrection, one judgment' structure (John 5:28-29; Matthew 25:31-46) shared with amillennialism.
Grounds missions, cultural labour and long-term institution-building in the conviction that faithful work in history will not be in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58).
Has deep roots in Reformed and Puritan tradition and in the theology that fuelled the Great Awakening and modern missions.
Reads the kingdom parables of growth (mustard seed, leaven) as describing a process that eventually dominates its environment, not one that remains marginal.

The New Testament predicts persecution, apostasy and worsening conditions before the end (Matthew 24:9-12; Luke 18:8; 2 Timothy 3:1-5), and the wheat and tares grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:24-30).

Postmillennialists answer that many such texts describe the apostolic generation before AD 70 (especially in preterist readings), that the wheat-and-tares parable shows coexistence, not proportions, and that the parables of the mustard seed and leaven immediately follow it to show the kingdom's eventual dominance. Victory comes through suffering, not instead of it.
History refutes it: the twentieth century's world wars, genocides and the secularisation of the West hardly look like a golden age dawning.

The view does not claim steady, unbroken progress; it works on a scale of centuries and millennia. Proponents point to Christianity's expansion from a small Jewish sect to a worldwide faith and to explosive growth in the Global South as evidence the leaven is still working, while Western decline is a reversal Scripture also anticipates for unfaithful churches (Revelation 2:5).
Postmillennialism is tied to theonomy or Christian nationalism and risks pursuing the kingdom through political power.

Many postmillennialists (Edwards, Hodge, Warfield, Iain Murray, Mathison) were not theonomists. All insist the engine of advance is the Spirit through the gospel; cultural transformation follows conversion and cannot be imposed. Reconstructionists themselves argue for change from the bottom up by regeneration, not top-down coercion.
Revelation 19-20 reads most naturally as a sequence: Christ returns (19:11-21) and then the millennium begins (20:1-6), which favours premillennialism.

Postmillennialists such as Warfield read Revelation 19:11-21 as a symbolic picture of the gospel's conquest (the rider fights with the sword from his mouth, his word), not the bodily return; others read it with preterists as Christ's judgment-coming in AD 70. Revelation 20 then recapitulates the age of gospel triumph.
If a long golden age must come first, the return of Christ cannot be imminent, which weakens New Testament exhortations to watchfulness.

Postmillennialists argue that biblical 'imminence' stresses certainty, suddenness and moral readiness rather than a possible return at any moment; Jesus himself spoke of a delay (Matthew 25:5, 19), and Peter of a Lord for whom a thousand years are as a day (2 Peter 3:8-9). Each believer should be ready to meet Christ at death or his coming.
Puritan / revivalist postmillennialism

The classic form found in the Puritans, Jonathan Edwards and the Princeton theologians: the latter-day glory comes chiefly through outpourings of the Spirit in revival, the preaching of the Word, prayer (Edwards' 'concerts of prayer'), missions and the conversion of the Jews. Cultural blessing follows as a by-product of widespread conversion. It is historicist in much of its reading of Revelation and generally does not tie the hope to a programme of civil law.
Reconstructionist / theonomic postmillennialism

Associated with R. J. Rushdoony, Greg Bahnsen, Gary North, David Chilton and (in its eschatology) Kenneth Gentry and Gary DeMar. It joins postmillennial optimism to theonomy, the conviction that God's moral law, including the abiding equity of Mosaic civil law, should shape every sphere of life, including civil government. Advocates stress that this transformation follows mass conversion and is pursued by persuasion, not force; critics, including other postmillennialists, dispute the theonomic application.
Preterist postmillennialism

Combines postmillennialism with partial preterism (Gentry, DeMar, Chilton, Mathison, Douglas Wilson). The Olivet Discourse's tribulation and most of Revelation are fulfilled in the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 (generally with an early, pre-70 date for Revelation, a dating that is disputed), clearing the way for the gospel's worldwide advance; Revelation 20 then describes the present church age, ending in the future bodily return of Christ.
Whole-age versus latter-day-glory postmillennialism

Postmillennialists disagree on the millennium's extent. Some (e.g. Gentry, Boettner) identify it with the entire period between the advents, a reign that grows progressively. Others, following Edwards and many Puritans, see the millennium as a future, distinct era of unusual blessing still to come within the present age, often after the conversion of Israel.
Amillennialism
Amil
The millennium is now: Christ reigns and Satan is bound between the two comings.

Amillennialists often dislike their own label, since 'a-millennial' suggests 'no millennium.' They affirm a real millennium, but a present one: an “inaugurated” or “realized millennium” (Jay Adams' preferred term, 'realized millennialism'), in which the risen Christ reigns from heaven, the souls of departed saints reign with him, and Satan is bound so that the gospel reaches the nations. They speak of “inaugurated eschatology”, the “already and not yet”, and the two-age structure of this age and the age to come.

Amillennialism teaches that the thousand years of Revelation 20 symbolise the whole period between Christ's first and second comings. Satan was bound by Christ's victory at the cross and resurrection so that he can no longer prevent the gospel from going to the nations; the 'first resurrection' refers to the believer's new birth and/or the reign of departed believers with Christ in heaven. History runs along two parallel tracks, the growth of the kingdom and the growth of evil, until a final apostasy and tribulation. Then Christ returns once, raises all the dead, judges all people and brings the new heavens and new earth. It has been the majority view in the Western church since Augustine and is held across Reformed, Lutheran, Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions.
The millennium (Revelation 20:1-6) is symbolic of the whole inter-advent age, beginning with Christ's death, resurrection and ascension and ending at his return.

Satan was bound at the first advent (Matthew 12:28-29; Luke 10:18; John 12:31-32; Colossians 2:15) in a specific respect: he cannot 'deceive the nations' so as to stop the gospel's worldwide spread, though he still opposes believers (1 Peter 5:8).

The 'first resurrection' is spiritual: regeneration (John 5:24-25; Ephesians 2:5-6) and/or the life and reign of believers' souls with Christ in the intermediate state (Revelation 20:4; 2 Corinthians 5:8).
The New Testament has a two-age structure: 'this age' and 'the age to come' (Matthew 12:32; Ephesians 1:21), with no third, intermediate earthly age between them.
There is one Second Coming, one general bodily resurrection of righteous and wicked together, and one final judgment (John 5:28-29; Acts 24:15; Matthew 25:31-46; 2 Thessalonians 1:6-10).

Good and evil coexist and mature together until the harvest (Matthew 13:24-30, 36-43); the age ends with a final apostasy, a climactic tribulation and the revealing of Antichrist (2 Thessalonians 2:3-8; Revelation 20:7-10).
Revelation is structured by recapitulation or 'progressive parallelism': its cycles (seals, trumpets, bowls, etc.) each cover the period between the advents, from different angles.
The Old Testament promises to Israel are fulfilled in Christ and his one people, Jew and Gentile, and consummated in the new creation, a renewed physical earth (Romans 8:18-23; Revelation 21-22).

Alongside the chiliasm of Papias, Justin and Irenaeus, a non-chiliast eschatology was present early; Justin himself acknowledged that many sincere Christians did not share his view (Dialogue with Trypho 80). Charles Hill argues that a belief that departed souls go at once to heaven correlated with non-chiliasm. Origen, Dionysius of Alexandria and later Tyconius (whose recapitulation approach to Revelation influenced Augustine) moved away from a literal earthly millennium.

In The City of God (book 20) Augustine, who earlier held a spiritualised chiliasm, identified the thousand years with the church age, Satan's binding with Christ's binding of the strong man, and the first resurrection with the soul's rising from sin. This reading dominated the medieval Western church.

Luther and Calvin, and the Lutheran and Reformed confessions, retained the Augustinian structure. The Augsburg Confession (Article 17) and Second Helvetic Confession (ch. 11) reject teaching of an earthly kingdom of the saints before the general resurrection; the Belgic and Westminster Confessions assume one general resurrection and judgment.

Dutch Reformed theologians (Abraham Kuyper, Herman Bavinck) and Geerhardus Vos, whose Pauline Eschatology set out the two-age framework, gave the view rigorous biblical-theological grounding. William Hendriksen's More Than Conquerors (1939) popularised progressive parallelism in Revelation, and Anthony Hoekema's The Bible and the Future (1979) emphasised 'inaugurated eschatology' and the new earth.

Major contemporary advocates include G. K. Beale (eclectic idealist commentary on Revelation), Dennis Johnson, Kim Riddlebarger, Sam Storms (a convert from dispensationalism), Samuel Waldron and many Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican scholars. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (676) rejects millenarianism, and Orthodox theology is broadly amillennial.
Simple, unified structure: one return, one resurrection, one judgment, which fits the many New Testament texts that place these together (John 5:28-29; 2 Thessalonians 1:6-10; Matthew 25:31-46).
Reads Revelation as apocalyptic literature, attentive to its pervasive symbolism and numerology and to its recapitulating structure.
Grounds the binding of Satan in the Gospels' own language of the strong man bound (Matthew 12:29) and the ruler of this world cast out (John 12:31).
Fits the New Testament's 'already/not yet' inaugurated eschatology and the two-age framework of Jesus and Paul.
Has the broadest historical and confessional support in the church since Augustine, across Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed traditions.
A bound Satan contradicts texts that portray him as active now: he prowls like a lion (1 Peter 5:8), blinds unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4) and is the god of this age.

The binding in Revelation 20:3 is limited in purpose, 'so that he might not deceive the nations any longer', which amillennialists take to mean he cannot prevent the gospel from going to the Gentiles. A chained dog can still be dangerous within the range of its chain. Jesus used the same binding language of his own ministry (Matthew 12:29, the same verb, deō).
The same verb, 'came to life' (ezēsan), is used of both groups in Revelation 20:4-5; if the second is a bodily resurrection, so is the first (Henry Alford's classic objection).

Amillennialists reply that John deliberately contrasts a 'first resurrection' with the 'second death', implying differences in kind; that John 5:25-29 uses resurrection language for both spiritual and bodily life in one passage; and that Revelation 20:4 describes 'souls', which suits the intermediate state of believers who live and reign with Christ.
Revelation 19-20 is a chronological sequence: the return of Christ (19:11-21) precedes the binding of Satan and the thousand years.

Amillennialists note that the battle of 20:7-10 replays the same final battle as 19:17-21 and 16:14-16, each drawing on Ezekiel 38-39 and each called 'the war' with the article. Revelation repeatedly returns to the beginning of the age (e.g. 12:1-6), so 20:1 begins a new cycle at the first advent.
It spiritualises Old Testament promises of an earthly kingdom, such as the wolf and lamb lying down (Isaiah 11:6-9; 65:17-25).

Amillennialists insist the fulfilment is physical, but in the new heavens and new earth, the context Isaiah 65:17 itself names, not in an interim age. They argue that the apostles read Israel's prophecies Christologically (e.g. Amos 9:11-12 in Acts 15:16-18), so following that apostolic hermeneutic is not arbitrary spiritualising.
Postmillennialists charge amillennialism with historical pessimism, expecting the church to remain a persecuted minority until the end.

Amillennialists answer that their view is profoundly victorious, since Christ reigns now and his people conquer through his blood and their testimony (Revelation 12:11). They do not predict how much the gospel will prosper, only that the church will suffer and that triumph is assured at Christ's return; some amillennialists are quite hopeful about gospel growth and a future conversion of Israel.
Realized millennialism

Jay E. Adams, in The Time Is at Hand (1966), proposed 'realized millennialism' as a more accurate name than 'amillennialism': the millennium is not denied but already realised in the present reign of Christ. Adams combined this with a largely preterist reading of Revelation, and reviewers differ on whether his view is better classed as amil or postmil. The term highlights the inaugurated-eschatology emphasis that most amillennialists share.
Heavenly-millennium (intermediate-state) amillennialism

Revelation 20:4-6 depicts the souls of deceased believers, especially martyrs, reigning with Christ in heaven during the inter-advent age; the first resurrection is the believer's entrance into this heavenly life at death. Associated with B. B. Warfield's essay on Revelation 20 (though Warfield was postmillennial elsewhere), William Hendriksen, Anthony Hoekema and Kim Riddlebarger. On this view the millennium is 'in heaven', while the binding of Satan is on earth.
Inaugurated new-creation amillennialism

Stresses that the resurrection of Jesus launched the new creation, that believers already share in it by regeneration (2 Corinthians 5:17), and that the final state is a renewed physical cosmos, not a disembodied heaven. Hoekema's chapter on the new earth and G. K. Beale's New Testament biblical theology are representative. It answers the charge that amillennialism 'spiritualises' the promises: the land and earthly promises are fulfilled concretely in the new earth.
Optimistic vs. pilgrim (two-kingdoms) amillennialism

Amillennialists differ over expectations for history. Some are hopeful about significant gospel growth and, following Romans 11:25-26, expect a future mass conversion of ethnic Israel (e.g. Riddlebarger, following Vos and John Murray's exegesis), sitting close to postmillennialism. Others (e.g. Hoekema, O. Palmer Robertson) read 'all Israel' as the full number of elect Jews through the age. A more pilgrim-minded strand (Meredith Kline's common-grace and two-kingdoms model; the Protestant Reformed tradition) expects the church to remain a pilgrim minority and sharply rejects postmillennial optimism.
Historic Premillennialism
Historic Premil
Christ returns after the tribulation to reign on earth before the final state.

Proponents call it “historic” or “classic” premillennialism to signal continuity with the earliest Christian chiliasts (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus) and to distinguish it from dispensationalism. Following George Ladd, they describe the kingdom as “the presence of the future”: already inaugurated in Jesus, yet awaiting a future, visible, earthly stage when Christ returns. Some Reformed advocates speak of “covenantal premillennialism.”

Historic premillennialism teaches that Christ will return visibly after a final tribulation, raise the righteous dead, and then reign on earth for a millennium (literal or symbolic in length) before the final rebellion, the resurrection of the rest of the dead, the last judgment and the eternal state. Unlike dispensationalism, it sees one people of God, holds that the church will pass through the tribulation (posttribulationism), and reads the Old Testament in the light of the New. It shares amillennialism's inaugurated eschatology but takes Revelation 19-20 as sequential and the first resurrection in Revelation 20:4-5 as bodily. Many historic premillennialists expect a future conversion of ethnic Israel (Romans 11:26).
The kingdom of God was inaugurated in Jesus' ministry, death and resurrection ('already') but will be consummated in stages at and after his return ('not yet').
Revelation 19:11-20:6 is sequential: the Second Coming is followed by the binding of Satan and a thousand-year reign of Christ with his saints on earth.

There are two bodily resurrections: the 'first resurrection' of believers at Christ's return (Revelation 20:4-6; 1 Corinthians 15:23) and a later resurrection of the rest of the dead for judgment (Revelation 20:5, 11-15).

The church passes through the great tribulation; the 'rapture' and the Second Coming are a single event after the tribulation (Matthew 24:29-31; 2 Thessalonians 2:1-8), the saints rising to meet and escort the returning king (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17).
There is one people of God, Jew and Gentile, in the one olive tree; Old Testament prophecy is read through New Testament fulfilment, not by a strict Israel-church distinction.
Many expect a future turning of ethnic Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25-27), often around the time of his return.
The millennium vindicates Christ's rule within history on a renewed earth; it ends with Satan's release, a final rebellion, the last judgment and the eternal new creation.
